# Blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses

> *A person can carry hepatitis B virus from birth, or HIV for a decade, feel well throughout, and
> pass the virus on in blood, during sex or to a child. Because these viruses spread silently for
> years, they are controlled by screening, sterile needles and vaccination more than by recognising
> illness.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why the blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses are controlled mainly by screening,
  sterile needles, vaccination and treatment of infected people.
- Describe how HIV passes between people, why a person in the window period can transmit it while
  an antibody test is negative, and how condoms, treatment and drugs taken before or after exposure
  prevent its spread.
- Explain why hepatitis B virus acquired at birth usually becomes chronic while infection in
  adulthood usually clears, and how the immune response damages the liver.
- Explain why antiviral drugs cure most hepatitis C virus infections but only suppress hepatitis B
  virus and HIV.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main virus cause disease.
- Tell hepatitis B virus from hepatitis C virus by genome, infectiousness in blood, effect of age at
  infection, and vaccine or cure.
:::

## The group {#sec-bbv-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-bbv-sentence}

The viruses in this group spread by blood, by sexual contact or from mother to child, and several of
them persist for years without symptoms while the infected person can transmit them. A
**blood-borne virus** is a virus that circulates in the blood and is transmitted by it, and a
**sexually transmitted infection** is an infection passed on mainly by sexual contact. The group is
defined by route, so its members differ in genome and structure (see [*A map of the
viruses*](virus-map.qmd)), and several of the six questions have a different answer for each virus.

The main viruses are hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV) and HIV, the viral anchor. HBV
and HCV are named for **hepatitis**, inflammation of the liver, which both cause. Human
papillomavirus (HPV) is a supporting member: it spreads by sexual contact but does not circulate in
the blood.

| Question | Answer for the blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | Different genomes: RNA that is copied into DNA (HIV), DNA that is copied through RNA (HBV), single-stranded **positive-sense RNA**, which ribosomes can translate directly (HCV), and double-stranded DNA (HPV); HIV, HBV and HCV are enveloped, HPV is not |
| How does it get energy? | It has no energy supply of its own and uses the host cell's |
| How does it copy itself and change? | HIV and HBV copy their genomes with a **reverse transcriptase**, a viral DNA polymerase that uses RNA as its template; HCV with its own **RNA-dependent RNA polymerase**, a viral enzyme that makes RNA from an RNA template; and HPV with the host cell's DNA polymerase (see [*How viruses are built and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). None of the three viral enzymes proofreads: HIV and HCV vary greatly, and HBV, whose genes overlap so that most changes damage more than one protein, varies less but still gives rise to drug-resistant variants. HPV, copied by a host polymerase that proofreads, changes slowly |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Humans are the only reservoir; HIV, HBV and HCV are carried in blood, semen and vaginal fluid, and spread by sexual contact, by blood and from mother to child; HPV stays in the skin and mucosa and spreads by skin-to-skin contact, including sexual contact |
| How does damage happen? | Slowly, over years to decades, often without symptoms: loss of **CD4 T cells**, the lymphocytes that coordinate the immune response (HIV); immune attack on infected liver cells, which can scar the liver and lead to liver cancer (HBV, HCV); changes in infected epithelial cells that can lead to cancer (HPV) |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | Viral enzymes and other proteins needed for replication: reverse transcriptase, integrase, which joins the DNA copy into a host chromosome, and protease, which cuts long viral proteins into their working parts (HIV); reverse transcriptase (HBV); RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, protease and a further replication protein that is not an enzyme (HCV); HPV, which uses the host cell's DNA polymerase, offers no target for current antiviral drugs |

Blood, semen, vaginal fluid and, for HIV, breast milk carry HIV, HBV and HCV from one person to the
next, by three routes (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)):

- Sexual contact, through the mucosa of the genital tract or rectum
- Blood, through shared needles and syringes, transfusion of unscreened blood, unsterile medical
  equipment or injury
- **Mother-to-child transmission** (vertical transmission), the spread of an infection from a
  mother to her child during pregnancy, at birth or in breast milk

HIV, HBV and HCV can each cause **chronic infection**, infection and inflammation continuing for
months or years, often without symptoms, and throughout that time the infected person's blood and
secretions carry virus (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-chronic)). Most
transmission therefore comes from people who feel well and may not know they are infected, and
waiting for illness finds infections too late to stop their spread.

::: {.example}
Without treatment, a person infected with HIV usually feels well for years, and throughout those
years the virus in blood and genital secretions can infect others.
:::

Control rests on **screening**, testing people who have no symptoms in order to find an infection
early, and on measures that block the routes of spread:

- Screening of donated blood and organs, and of pregnant women
- Sterile, single-use needles and syringes in medical care, and sterile injecting equipment for
  people who inject drugs
- Vaccination against HBV and HPV
- Condoms, and treatment of infected people, which lowers the amount of virus they can pass on

Health workers meet these viruses through a **needlestick injury**, a puncture of the skin by a
needle that has been used on a patient, or a splash of blood onto mucosa; vaccination protects them
against HBV, the most infectious of the three in blood, and drugs started soon after an exposure
lower the risk of HIV infection.

### Sorting the group {#sec-bbv-key}

We sort the group first by the cells each virus infects, because the target cell predicts the
disease. For the two viruses that infect liver cells, we then ask whether the virus keeps a DNA copy
of its genome in the nucleus, because that predicts whether drugs can cure the infection.

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the blood-borne and sexually transmitted viruses]{.tree-title}

- CD4 T cells and macrophages: HIV
- Liver cells
  - A DNA genome, copied through RNA; a DNA copy stays in the nucleus: hepatitis B virus
  - An RNA genome, copied in the cytoplasm with no DNA stage: hepatitis C virus
- Basal cells of the epithelium of the skin and mucosa: human papillomavirus
:::

The cells a virus infects predict what follows and how it is prevented:

| Cells infected | What follows | Main means of prevention |
|---|---|---|
| CD4 T cells and macrophages | Over years, CD4 T cells are lost, the defences they coordinate fail, and organisms normally held in check cause disease | Condoms, treatment of infected people, drugs taken before or after exposure, screened blood and sterile needles |
| Liver cells | Hepatitis; chronic infection can scar the liver and lead to liver cancer over decades | Screened blood, sterile needles and, for HBV, vaccination |
| Basal cells of the epithelium of the skin and genital tract | Warts; persistent infection with some types can lead, over years, to cancer of the cervix and other sites | Vaccination, and screening of the cervix |

The second trait predicts what antiviral drugs can do. The drugs block viral enzymes and other viral
proteins needed for replication, and act only on virus that is replicating (see [*Detecting viruses
and antiviral targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-few)), so viral DNA that sits in the nucleus
without needing those proteins is out of their reach.

| Virus | What stays in the nucleus of an infected cell | What antiviral drugs can do |
|---|---|---|
| HIV | Its DNA copy, joined into a host chromosome, including in resting CD4 T cells that make no virus | Suppress replication while they are taken, so treatment continues for life |
| HBV | A DNA copy of the genome, kept as a closed circle beside the chromosomes | Suppress replication, but rarely clear the infection |
| HCV | Nothing: the RNA genome is copied in the cytoplasm and never made into DNA | Cure most infections in a few months |

Work through the key from the cells the virus infects, and read at each branch what the trait
predicts about the virus.

## Main viruses {#sec-bbv-main}

### HIV: silent spread, and treatment for life {#sec-bbv-hiv}

HIV is an enveloped **retrovirus**, an RNA virus that copies its genome into DNA inside the cell. It
binds CD4 and a co-receptor, so it infects CD4 T cells and macrophages (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-receptors)). Reverse transcriptase copies its RNA genome into DNA,
and integrase joins that DNA into a host chromosome as a **provirus**, viral DNA integrated into a
host chromosome, transcribed by the host and copied with the chromosome (see [*How viruses are built
and copy themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). Over years the loss of
CD4 T cells lets **cell-mediated immunity**, the defence by T cells against infected cells and
against organisms that live inside host cells, fail, and **opportunistic infections**, infections by
organisms that a person with intact defences controls, then cause disease (see [*Viruses and the
host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cd4)).

HIV is carried in blood, semen, vaginal fluid, rectal secretions and breast milk, and it spreads by
all three routes of the group:

- Sexual contact, the commonest route worldwide
- Blood, mainly through needles and syringes shared by people who inject drugs, and rarely through a
  needlestick injury
- From mother to child, mostly at birth or in breast milk and less often across the placenta during
  pregnancy

The risk from an exposure rises with the **viral load** of the infected person, the amount of viral
nucleic acid in a sample, usually plasma, measured by a quantitative NAAT (nucleic acid
amplification test; see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-methods)). HIV is not spread by everyday contact, by sharing
food or cutlery, or by mosquitoes.

In the first weeks after infection the virus multiplies rapidly in lymphoid tissue, and the viral
load reaches its highest level. Some people have a short illness with fever, sore throat, rash and
enlarged lymph nodes; others notice nothing. The immune response then lowers the viral load to a
steady level, and years without symptoms follow, while virus is produced continuously and CD4 T cells
are slowly lost (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-chronic)). Without treatment,
the **acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS)**, the advanced stage of HIV infection in which loss
of CD4 T cells lets opportunistic infections cause disease, develops after about ten years on
average.

Antibody tests detect infection only once antibodies have formed, some weeks after infection. The
**window period** is the interval after infection in which an infected person still tests negative
because antibodies have not yet appeared. It overlaps the weeks of highest viral load, so a person
can be at their most infectious while an antibody test is still negative. Tests that detect a viral
protein alongside antibodies shorten the window period, and a NAAT for HIV RNA shortens it further
(see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-choosing)).

HIV harms the host mainly through the cells it destroys:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Early illness | The virus multiplies rapidly in lymphoid tissue and the blood, and the host's response to it causes fever and enlarged lymph nodes | Fever, sore throat, rash and enlarged lymph nodes two to four weeks after infection, when an antibody test may still be negative |
| Failure of cell-mediated immunity | Over years, CD4 T cells are killed faster than they are replaced, until cell-mediated immunity fails | Tuberculosis in a person with advanced HIV infection, because the control of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* inside macrophages depends on cell-mediated immunity |
| Cancers caused by other viruses | Failing cell-mediated immunity no longer holds in check cells infected by viruses that can cause cancer | Cancer of the cervix, caused by HPV, which develops more often in women with HIV |

Three conditions let HIV cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone exposed without protection; no vaccine exists | The immune response does not clear HIV, which persists as a provirus, so every infection is lifelong |
| Where (setting) | Sex without a condom with a partner whose infection is undiagnosed or untreated; shared injecting equipment; pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding when the mother is not treated | The amount of virus in blood and genital secretions follows the viral load, which is highest early in infection and in untreated infection |
| How (route) | Through the mucosa of the genital tract or rectum, or directly into the blood | It infects CD4 T cells and macrophages, is carried in lymph to the lymph nodes and then in the blood to lymphoid tissue throughout the body |

HIV infection is prevented by blocking a route, by lowering the amount of virus an infected person
carries, or by protecting the person who is exposed:

- Condoms, which block contact with semen and vaginal fluid
- Treatment of the infected person, which lowers the viral load in blood and genital secretions; when
  it has kept the viral load below the level tests can detect for at least six months, HIV is not
  transmitted sexually
- **Pre-exposure prophylaxis** (PrEP), drugs against HIV taken by a person without HIV who may be
  exposed, before the exposure
- **Post-exposure prophylaxis** (PEP), a short course of drugs against HIV started as soon as
  possible after an exposure, such as a needlestick injury or sex without a condom
- Screening of donated blood, and sterile injecting equipment
- Treatment of pregnant women with HIV, and drugs for their infants after birth, which make
  transmission to the child rare

**Antiretroviral therapy** is the treatment of HIV infection with a combination of drugs from two or
more classes, acting on different steps of the replication cycle, so that a variant resistant to one
drug is still suppressed by the others (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-resistance)). It suppresses replication and lets the CD4
T-cell count recover, and a person who starts it early and takes it consistently can expect a
near-normal lifespan. It cannot remove the provirus from resting CD4 T cells, which make no virus and
offer the drugs nothing to act on (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-latency)).
When treatment stops, virus returns from these cells within weeks, so treatment continues for life.
The variation of HIV, within one person and between people, is one reason why no vaccine has yet
succeeded (see [*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-vaccines)).

::: {.callout-important}
## Can a person taking HIV treatment pass the virus on during sex?
HIV is often assumed to be infectious for as long as a person carries it, because the infection is
never cleared. Yet among couples in which only one partner had HIV, followed through many thousands
of acts of sex without condoms, no infection has been traced to a partner whose treatment had kept
the viral load undetectable for at least six months. The provirus persists, but the cells that carry
it release little virus, the drugs stop that virus from infecting new cells, and so there is too
little virus in blood and genital secretions to pass on during sex.

The evidence concerns sexual transmission. In breastfeeding and through shared needles, treatment
lowers the risk, but it has not been shown to remove it.
:::

Step through the two routes HIV takes: sexual transmission and the slow loss of CD4 T cells that
follows, and transmission from mother to child.

### Hepatitis B virus: age at infection decides the outcome {#sec-bbv-hbv}

HBV is an enveloped virus that infects liver cells. Its genome is a small, partly double-stranded
DNA molecule, which it copies in an unusual way. In the nucleus of the liver cell, the genome is
completed into a closed circle of DNA, which stays there beside the chromosomes. Host RNA polymerase
transcribes the circle, and in the cytoplasm a viral reverse transcriptase copies one of its RNA
transcripts back into DNA, making the genomes of new virions. HBV and HIV therefore both use a
reverse transcriptase, but HIV copies RNA into DNA soon after it enters a cell, whereas HBV does so
as it makes new virions.

The blood of a person with HBV infection can contain far more virus than the blood of a person with
HIV or HCV infection, and HBV remains infectious in dried blood on surfaces for at least a week.
Small amounts of blood can therefore transmit it, on a needle, a shared razor or toothbrush, or
unsterile medical or dental equipment. It also spreads by sexual contact, among young children in a
household, and from mother to child at birth, the main route in East and South-East Asia, where
chronic infection is common. HBV is not spread by sharing food or cutlery, by hugging, by coughing or
by breastfeeding.

Infected liver cells make the main protein of the viral envelope, **hepatitis B surface antigen**
(HBsAg), in far greater amounts than are needed to build virions, and release the excess into the
blood. HBsAg in the blood therefore marks current infection, and a test for it is the usual way
infection is found. Antibodies against HBsAg appear when the infection clears and after vaccination,
and they protect against infection.

The age at which a person is infected decides whether the infection clears or becomes chronic.
Chronic HBV infection is recognised by HBsAg that persists in the blood for more than six months.

::: {.spectrum}
[Chance that HBV infection becomes chronic, by age at infection]{.tree-title}

- At birth or in the first year of life: about 9 in 10
- In early childhood, before the age of six: between a third and a half
- In healthy adults: fewer than 1 in 20

[Birth]{.spectrum-end} [Adulthood]{.spectrum-end}
:::

HBV itself kills few of the cells it infects. The liver damage comes mainly from
**cytotoxic T cells**, lymphocytes that recognise viral proteins displayed on an infected cell and
kill that cell (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-immune)). An infant's immune
response does not attack infected liver cells strongly enough to clear them, so the virus persists,
often for years with little damage to the liver. In an adult, the attack that clears the virus
within months also causes acute hepatitis, which is often silent but can bring fatigue and
**jaundice**, yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes as bilirubin accumulates in the
blood. The strength of the response therefore decides both whether the virus is cleared and how much
damage is done (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-drf)).

::: {.example}
An infant infected with HBV at birth usually has no illness at all, while an infected adult can
become jaundiced; the infant's silent infection is the one that persists, and decades later it can
lead to liver cancer.
:::

In chronic infection, the immune response can attack infected liver cells, on and off, for decades
without clearing them. The injured cells are replaced by regenerating ones, and the repeated injury
lays down scar tissue. **Cirrhosis** is scarring of the liver in which bands of fibrous tissue and
nodules of regenerating liver cells replace its normal structure, so that the liver works poorly, and
**hepatocellular carcinoma** is a cancer of liver cells. Many people with chronic infection spend
long periods with little damage to the liver, but in a substantial minority both follow, and
hepatocellular carcinoma can arise even in a liver without cirrhosis. Chronic HBV infection is a
leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma in East and South-East Asia.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Acute hepatitis | Cytotoxic T cells kill infected liver cells as they clear the virus | Fatigue and jaundice in an unvaccinated adult, two months after sex with an infected partner, settling over the following months |
| Chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis | The immune response attacks infected liver cells, on and off, for decades without clearing them, and repeated injury and repair scar the liver | Cirrhosis in a middle-aged adult who was infected at birth |
| Hepatocellular carcinoma | Decades of liver cell death and regeneration, during which fragments of HBV DNA can become inserted into the chromosomes of liver cells, allow cancer to develop | Hepatocellular carcinoma in a 45-year-old who was infected at birth and whose liver has no cirrhosis |

Three conditions let HBV cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | An infant born to a mother with chronic infection; anyone who is unvaccinated | An infant's immune response rarely clears the virus, so infection at birth usually becomes chronic; vaccination prevents infection at any age |
| Where (setting) | Birth to an infected mother, especially in East and South-East Asia; sexual contact; shared needles, razors or toothbrushes; unsterile medical equipment | The blood carries very large amounts of virus, which remains infectious in dried blood for at least a week |
| How (route) | Through mucosa or broken skin, or directly into the blood, then in the blood to the liver | Liver cells carry the receptor the virus binds, so it infects them and few other cells |

The vaccine contains HBsAg alone, made without the virus, and the antibodies it induces prevent
infection. Infection at birth is the one most likely to persist, so the first dose is given at birth,
as it is in Singapore's national childhood immunisation schedule. Pregnant women are screened for
HBsAg, and an infant whose mother has chronic infection is given the vaccine together with antibodies
against HBV within hours of birth, which prevents most transmission. When the mother's viral load is
very high, transmission can still occur despite these, so she is also given drugs that block the
reverse transcriptase of HBV in the last months of pregnancy. By preventing chronic infection, the
vaccine prevents much of the hepatocellular carcinoma that would otherwise follow decades later.

Drugs that block the reverse transcriptase of HBV stop new DNA genomes being made, which suppresses
the virus and slows damage to the liver. The circle of DNA already in the nucleus does not depend on
the reverse transcriptase, however, so it stays in the cell, and virus often returns when the drugs
are stopped. The drugs therefore rarely clear the infection, and treatment usually continues for
years.

Step through the two routes by which HBV reaches the liver: at birth, when the infection usually
becomes chronic, and in adulthood, when it usually clears.

### Hepatitis C virus: silent for decades, and curable {#sec-bbv-hcv}

HCV is an enveloped virus with a positive-sense RNA genome. Host ribosomes translate the genome as
soon as it enters a liver cell, and the virus's own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies it in the
cytoplasm (see [*How viruses are built and copy
themselves*](virus-structure-replication.qmd#sec-vstr-genomes)). HCV makes no DNA at any stage. Its
polymerase does not proofread, so the virus in one person becomes a population of many variants (see
[*How viruses change*](virus-change.qmd#sec-vchg-mutation)).

HCV is spread mainly by blood. In many countries most new infections now come from needles, syringes
and other equipment shared by people who inject drugs. In the past, many people were infected by
transfusion of blood before donations were screened for HCV, or by medical procedures with unsterile
equipment, and the virus still spreads in this way where infection control is poor. Sexual and
mother-to-child transmission occur but are much less efficient than for HBV or HIV, although sexual
transmission is a recognised route of new infection among men who have sex with men, particularly
those with HIV.

Acute infection usually causes no symptoms, and most infections, about 7 in 10, are not cleared and
become chronic. Chronic infection is usually silent while inflammation slowly scars the liver. Over
two or three decades a substantial minority of people with chronic infection develop cirrhosis, and
some of them develop hepatocellular carcinoma. Many people are therefore diagnosed only when their
liver disease is advanced, or when they are tested because of a past risk, such as injecting drugs or
a transfusion before blood was screened.

Antibodies against HCV show that a person has been infected at some time, but they remain after the
virus has gone, whether the immune response or treatment cleared it. A NAAT for HCV RNA shows whether
the virus is still present (see [*Detecting viruses and antiviral
targets*](detecting-viruses.qmd#sec-vdet-methods)).

HCV harms the liver slowly, through inflammation that does not clear the virus:

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Chronic hepatitis | The immune response fails to clear the virus, and infected liver cells are attacked by continuing, low-grade inflammation for years | No symptoms for decades in a person infected while injecting drugs as a young adult |
| Cirrhosis | Decades of inflammation lay down scar tissue throughout the liver | Cirrhosis found in a 60-year-old who was given a transfusion before blood was screened for HCV |
| Hepatocellular carcinoma | Cancer develops in a liver scarred by decades of inflammation, mostly after cirrhosis has formed | Hepatocellular carcinoma in a 65-year-old who has had cirrhosis from chronic HCV infection for several years |

Three conditions let HCV cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person exposed to infected blood, most often while injecting drugs; in the past, a person given unscreened blood | Most infections become chronic, and neither past infection nor cure reliably protects against reinfection |
| Where (setting) | Shared needles, syringes and other injecting equipment; unscreened blood and unsterile medical equipment where infection control is poor | Infected people carry virus in their blood for decades, usually without knowing it |
| How (route) | Directly into the blood, then in the blood to the liver | The virus infects liver cells and copies its RNA in their cytoplasm |

No vaccine against HCV exists; one obstacle is its genome, which varies greatly between people and
within each infected person. Neither recovery nor cure reliably protects against a new infection, so
people who continue to be exposed can be infected again.

Antiviral drugs that act on the virus's own enzymes and proteins, including its RNA-dependent RNA
polymerase and its protease, cure most infections when taken for a few months. HCV can be cured where
HIV and HBV can only be suppressed because it keeps no DNA copy in the nucleus and has no latent
form. It persists only by replicating continuously, so when drugs stop its replication for long
enough, the viral RNA already in infected cells is broken down and nothing remains from which the
virus can return.

Step through the route HCV takes, from a shared needle to a liver scarred over decades.

## Contrast pair {#sec-bbv-pairs}

### Hepatitis B virus and hepatitis C virus {#sec-bbv-pair-hbv-hcv}

HBV and HCV both infect liver cells, both spread in blood, and both can lead, after decades, to
cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Compare them feature by feature before reading the
principle.

## Beyond the main viruses {#sec-bbv-beyond}

### Supporting viruses {#sec-bbv-supporting}

| Virus | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| Human papillomavirus | The basal cells of the epithelium of the skin, and of the mucosa of the genital tract, anus and throat | A non-enveloped DNA virus that stays in the epithelium and does not circulate in the blood; spread by skin-to-skin contact, including sexual contact; there are many types, and most infections clear within one to two years | Some types cause warts on the skin or genitals. Persistent infection with high-risk types causes almost all cancers of the cervix and most cancers of the anus, and some cancers of the other genital organs and of the throat: two viral proteins inactivate the cell's tumour-suppressor proteins (see [*Viruses and the host*](virus-host.qmd#sec-vhost-cancer)). A vaccine given before sexual activity begins prevents infection with the main high-risk types, and screening of the cervix finds precancerous changes, which can be removed before cancer develops |

### Later in the course {#sec-bbv-later}

| Virus | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| HIV | Infectious diseases and HIV care (opportunistic infections and antiretroviral therapy); sexual health; obstetrics and neonatology (prevention of mother-to-child transmission); occupational health (needlestick injury) |
| Hepatitis B virus | Gastroenterology and hepatology (chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma); obstetrics and neonatology (vaccination at birth); vaccines in immunology |
| Hepatitis C virus | Gastroenterology and hepatology (chronic hepatitis and its cure); transfusion medicine (screening of donated blood) |
| Human papillomavirus | Obstetrics and gynaecology (cervical screening and cancer); dermatology and sexual health (warts); head-and-neck oncology |
